claims.claim: Every source is created by someone with a point of view, so every source carries a perspective shaped by who the author was, when and where they lived, and why they wrote.

Historians cannot wholly disconnect themselves from their own environment and beliefs, so historical writing is interpretive; bias can even act as a positive force by prompting historians to ask new questions, as when scholars in the 1960s-70s turned from elites to ordinary people.
Evaluating a source means asking who authored it and why, whether the author is reliable or has an agenda, for whom it was written, and whether other sources corroborate it.

The SHEG sourcing skill directs students to ask 'What is the author's perspective?' and to evaluate a source's trustworthiness by considering its genre, audience, and purpose; corroboration means comparing documents to recognize disparities between accounts.

Written records often leave out ordinary people, women, the poor, and minority communities, and some records were deliberately destroyed, as when conquerors in the Americas destroyed Indigenous writing tied to a religion and culture they meant to replace; identifying whose voices are missing is part of analysis.

The Library of Congress analysis routine has students observe, reflect, and question a source, asking who the intended audience was and why someone made the item, and comparing related sources to see how they support or challenge one another.

Recognizing that every account has a perspective does not make all accounts equally reliable; the danger lies in using only one lens, and bringing more strands of history together produces a more accurate picture.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether bias is purely a defect or can be useful
positions: Bias is a distortion that unfairly favors one side and should be identified and corrected for
A historian's standpoint (a form of bias) can be a positive force that surfaces overlooked questions and previously ignored people
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both hold at different scales: an individual source's bias must be weighed and corrected for, while the discipline benefits from diverse standpoints that together yield a fuller picture. The lesson keeps the distinction between unavoidable perspective and unfair distortion.
